topic.title: Collision theory: temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Question 7 of the C2 paper, usually beside the rate graph, typically 7-9 marks: a state-and-explain on temperature [3], the name of the catalyst [1] and a state-and-explain on the catalyst [3]. Outcomes 2.3.4 and 2.3.6 are Higher only; 2.3.5, the definition of a catalyst, is set at both tiers.
mustMemorise: Activation energy is the minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur
A successful collision is one with energy at or above the activation energy
Temperature: more frequent collisions AND a greater proportion with enough energy
Concentration and surface area: more frequent collisions
Always write more or fewer successful collisions per unit time
A catalyst increases the rate without being used up; transition metals and their compounds are often catalysts
Manganese(IV) oxide is the catalyst for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide
Higher: a catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy
A catalyst alters neither the energy change nor the amount of product

given: Relative atomic masses and the Periodic Table (Chemistry Data Leaflet)

mustKnow: Activation energy: the minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur
Temperature: more frequent collisions and a greater proportion with energy at or above the activation energy
Concentration and surface area: more frequent collisions
A catalyst: increases the rate without being used up
Higher: an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy

notOnThisSpec: Pressure of a reacting gas as a factor
Enzymes as catalysts, which belong to B1

mustBeAbleTo: Define activation energy as the minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur
Say what makes a collision successful
Explain a temperature change with both ideas: frequency and the proportion with enough energy
Explain a concentration or surface-area change with frequency alone
Write 'more (or fewer) successful collisions per unit time' in every explanation
Calculate a surface area to volume ratio and use it in an explanation
Define a catalyst and say what kind of substance catalysts usually are
Name manganese(IV) oxide as the catalyst for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide
Explain catalytic action as an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy (Higher)
Identify a catalyst from a table of masses before and after
Say why a catalyst changes neither the energy change nor the amount of product
Read a reaction profile with and without a catalyst and label the activation energy and the energy change
sheet.howExamined: C2, 1 hour 15 minutes, 70 marks at Foundation and 80 at Higher, with a calculator and the Chemistry Data Leaflet. Collision theory sits in Question 7 beside the rate graph. The shape repeats: a state-the-effect-then-explain-it question about temperature is [3] — one mark for the effect, one for what the particles do, one for the successful collisions; naming the catalyst for hydrogen peroxide is [1]; a state-the-effect-then-explain-it question about a catalyst is [3], with the effect [1], the alternative pathway [1] and the lower activation energy [1]. Outcomes 2.3.4 and 2.3.6 are Higher only.
traps: 'Less collisions' or 'more collisions' written without the word successful, which earned nothing in Summer 2025 (C2 H Q7)
'Per unit time' left out, which candidates are expected to include from the next series (Summer 2025 C2 H Q7)
The definition of a catalyst given where the question asked for its effect on the rate (Summer 2025 C2 H Q7)
Manganese(IV) oxide not recalled, although it has been asked in several series (Summer 2025 C2 H Q7, Summer 2023 C2 F Q6)
Activation energy described as the energy the reaction gives out (Summer 2023 C2 H Q2)
A catalyst said to lower the energy change, or to move the product level on the profile
A faster reaction said to produce more product
A catalyst said to be used up slowly, or written into the balanced equation
A concentration answer given the temperature explanation (particles moving faster)
Surface area described as the size of the lump rather than the surface area to volume ratio
Oxygen said to relight a lit splint rather than a glowing one (Summer 2023 C2 F Q6 and C2 H Q6)

steps.working: Effect: the rate of reaction increases.
steps.decision: Answer the 'state' part first and in one clause. It is a separate mark, and an explanation with no effect stated loses it.

steps.working: There are more acid particles in the same volume of solution.
steps.decision: Start the explanation with what has changed about the particles themselves. Concentration means how many particles are packed into the same space.

options: Because concentration is the number of particles in a given volume
Because concentrated acid particles are larger
Because concentrated acid particles move faster
whyMenu.explain: Only the number in the space changes. Making the particles faster is what heating does, and it is a different mark.

steps.working: So the particles collide more frequently, and there are more successful collisions per unit time.
steps.decision: Two words carry this mark: successful, and per unit time. 'More collisions' on its own was not credited in Summer 2025. Note that concentration changes only how often they collide, not how hard, so there is no energy line here.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) The rate of reaction increases. (b) There are more acid particles in the same volume, so the particles collide more frequently and there are more successful collisions per unit time.

twin.stem: The same reaction is repeated using powdered marble instead of chips, with the same mass of marble. State and explain the effect on the rate.

accepted: the rate increases because the powder has a larger surface area, so there are more frequent collisions and more successful collisions per unit time
the rate of reaction increases: a bigger surface area means more frequent collisions and more successful collisions each second

workedExamples.stem:
Hydrogen peroxide solution decomposes slowly to water and oxygen. A black powder is added and the mixture fizzes strongly. At the end the powder is filtered off, dried and weighed; its mass has not changed.
(a) Name the black powder. [1]
(b) State and explain the effect it has on this reaction. [3]
(c) Explain how the results of the weighing support your answer to (a). [1]

figure.alt: A watch glass of fine black manganese(IV) oxide powder.
figure.credit: W. Oelen, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
figure.prompt: What would the balance read after the reaction, and why?

steps.working: The black powder is manganese(IV) oxide.
steps.decision: Give the full name with its oxidation number. It is the one catalyst CCEA names, and Summer 2025's report called it surprising how few could recall it.

steps.working: Effect: it increases the rate of decomposition of the hydrogen peroxide.
steps.decision: 'State' wants the effect on the rate, in one clause. Writing the definition of a catalyst here instead is the error the 2025 report names.

options: Because the question asks what it does to the reaction, not what a catalyst is
Because the definition is worth more marks
Because a catalyst has no effect on the rate
whyMenu.explain: Definition and effect are two different questions. Read which one is being asked, and answer that one.

steps.working: Explanation: it provides an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy.
steps.decision: Two marks live in that one sentence: alternative pathway, and lower activation energy. Say both.

steps.working: Its mass is unchanged at the end, so it has not been used up — which is what a catalyst does.
steps.decision: The data is the evidence. A catalyst is recovered chemically unchanged and with the same mass, and it does not appear in the equation.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) Manganese(IV) oxide. (b) It increases the rate of decomposition, because it provides an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy. (c) Its mass is the same at the end, so it has not been used up.

twin.stem: A catalyst is added to a reaction that produces hydrogen gas. Explain why the total volume of hydrogen collected is unchanged.

accepted: the catalyst only changes how fast the reaction goes, and the amounts of reactant are unchanged, so the same volume of hydrogen is made
the amounts of reactants are the same and a catalyst changes only the rate, so the same amount of hydrogen is produced

steps.working: Each small cube has side 1 cm, so its surface area is 6 × 1² = 6 cm².
steps.decision: Work out one small cube first. Six faces, each a square of the small side.
Multiply by the number of pieces. The whole cube had only 24 cm², so cutting has doubled the area without adding any substance.

steps.working: Volume is unchanged: 2³ = 8 cm³ before, and 8 × 1 = 8 cm³ after.
steps.decision: Check the volume rather than assuming it. Nothing is added or lost by cutting, which is the point of the comparison.

steps.working: Ratios: 24 ÷ 8 = 3 cm⁻¹ before, and 48 ÷ 8 = 6 cm⁻¹ after.
steps.decision: Surface area on top, volume underneath. Turning the fraction over gives a number that falls when the pieces get smaller, which is the wrong way round.

steps.working: More of the calcium carbonate is exposed, so acid particles collide with its surface more frequently, and there are more successful collisions per unit time.
steps.decision: Finish in collision language. The ratio is the evidence; the collisions are the explanation.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) 48 cm². (b) 3 cm⁻¹ before and 6 cm⁻¹ after. (c) A larger surface area to volume ratio exposes more of the solid, so collisions with the acid are more frequent and there are more successful collisions per unit time.

items.stem: In a solid, a liquid and a gas, what are the particles doing?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 — particle theory; you are not expected to have met collision theory yet

options.text: always moving, even in a solid
options.feedback: Always moving. In a solid they vibrate in place; in a liquid and a gas they travel. This lesson is built on that movement.

options.text: still in a solid, moving in a liquid and a gas
options.feedback: Particles in a solid vibrate rather than travel, but they are never still. Section 1 of the lesson needs them moving.

options.text: only moving when the substance is heated
options.feedback: Heating makes them move faster, not start moving. They are moving at every temperature.

items.stem: Which of these is a rate of reaction, rather than an amount?
items.skill: Prerequisite from c2-measuring-rates — what a rate is

options.text: 0.64 cm³ of gas per second
options.feedback: A rate is an amount in each second, so it always carries a time in its unit.

options.text: 54 cm³ of gas
options.feedback: That is a total volume, with no time in it. A rate needs the time underneath.

options.text: 50 seconds
options.feedback: That is a time on its own. A rate is an amount divided by a time.

items.stem: What is the surface area of a cube of side 2 cm?
items.skill: Prerequisite from mathematics — surface area of a cube

options.text: 24 cm²
options.feedback: Six faces, each 2 × 2 = 4 cm², so 24 cm². Section 2 uses this to compare a lump with a powder.

options.text: 8 cm²
options.feedback: That is the volume, 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cm³, and it is measured in cm³, not cm². The surface area adds up the six faces.

options.text: 4 cm²
options.feedback: That is one face. A cube has six of them.

items.stem: What is meant by the activation energy of a reaction?

options.text: the minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur
options.feedback: A threshold on the way in. A collision with less than this much energy does nothing.

options.text: the energy given out by the reaction
options.feedback: That is the energy change, which is the drop between the reactant and the product levels. Activation energy is the hump on the way there.

options.text: the energy every collision has
options.feedback: Collisions have a range of energies, which is exactly why only some of them succeed.

options.text: the energy needed to make a catalyst work
options.feedback: A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so the idea exists with or without one.

items.stem: The temperature of a reaction mixture is raised. Which answer would the mark scheme credit in full?

options.text: the particles have more energy, so there are more successful collisions per unit time
options.feedback: Energy first, then successful collisions per unit time. That is the full three-mark shape.

options.text: there are more collisions
options.feedback: 'More collisions' on its own is the phrasing Summer 2025 refused to credit. The mark is in the word successful, and now in per unit time.

options.text: the particles get bigger, so they hit each other more
options.feedback: Heating does not change the size of a particle. It changes how fast it moves, and that is what the answer must say.

options.text: the activation energy is lowered
options.feedback: Only a catalyst lowers the activation energy. Heating gets more particles over the bar, it does not move the bar.

items.stem: A solution is made more concentrated. Which single idea explains the faster rate?

options.text: more particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent
options.feedback: Frequency only. Concentration does not change how hard the particles hit, which is why it is worth fewer marks than temperature.

options.text: the particles move faster, so they collide harder
options.feedback: That is the temperature explanation. Concentration changes how many particles are in the space, not how fast they move.

options.text: the activation energy falls
options.feedback: Only a catalyst does that. Concentration leaves the activation energy exactly where it was.

options.text: the reaction makes more product
options.feedback: A faster reaction makes the same product sooner. How much is made depends on the amounts of reactant.

items.stem: Which statement about a catalyst is correct?

options.text: it increases the rate and is not used up
options.feedback: Both halves matter: it speeds the reaction, and it is there at the end with the same mass.

options.text: it increases the rate and is slowly used up
options.feedback: A catalyst is recovered chemically unchanged and with the same mass. That is how a data question identifies it.

options.text: it increases the amount of product formed
options.feedback: The same amounts of reactant make the same amount of product; the catalyst only changes how long it takes.

options.text: it appears on the left of the balanced equation
options.feedback: A catalyst is not a reactant, so it is not in the equation. It is written above the arrow when it is shown at all.

items.stem: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?

options.text: it provides an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy
options.feedback: The sentence the mark scheme prints, and it is worth two of the three marks on this part.

options.text: it gives the particles more energy
options.feedback: That is what heating does. A catalyst lowers the bar instead of raising the particles.

options.text: it makes the particles collide more often
options.feedback: The collisions are just as frequent. More of them succeed, because less energy is needed.

options.text: it increases the energy change of the reaction
options.feedback: The energy change is fixed by the reactants and products, and a catalyst leaves both ends of the profile exactly where they were.

items.stem: A cube of side 2 cm is cut into 8 equal cubes. What happens to the surface area and the volume?

options.text: the surface area doubles to 48 cm² and the volume stays at 8 cm³
options.feedback: Cutting exposes faces that were inside. Nothing is added, so the volume is still 8 cm³ and the ratio rises from 3 to 6 cm⁻¹.

options.text: the surface area stays at 24 cm² and the volume stays at 8 cm³
options.feedback: Every cut makes two new faces that were not exposed before, so the total area goes up even though the solid is the same.

options.text: the surface area is 6 cm² and the volume stays at 8 cm³
options.feedback: That is the area of one small cube. There are 8 of them.

options.text: both the surface area and the volume double
options.feedback: Cutting cannot make more substance. The volume is unchanged, and that is what makes the ratio the interesting number.

items.stem: A reaction is repeated with a catalyst. Everything else is the same. What happens to the total volume of gas collected?

options.text: it is unchanged, but it is collected sooner
options.feedback: The amounts of reactant fix the amount of product. A catalyst changes only the time it takes.

options.text: it is larger, because the reaction is faster
options.feedback: Faster is not more. On a graph the new curve is steeper but levels off at exactly the same height.

options.text: it is smaller, because the catalyst uses some up
options.feedback: A catalyst is not used up and is not a reactant, so it takes nothing away from the product.

options.text: it depends on how much catalyst is added
options.feedback: More catalyst can make the reaction faster still, but the amount of product is set by the reactants.

items.stem: Which type of substance is most often used as a catalyst?
items.skill: Recall the kind of substance catalysts are

options.text: transition metals and their compounds
options.feedback: The specification's own words, and manganese(IV) oxide for hydrogen peroxide is the named example.

options.text: Group 1 metals
options.feedback: Group 1 metals react violently with water rather than catalysing things. The catalysts are the transition metals.

options.text: noble gases
options.feedback: Group 0 gases are unreactive and take no part at all, which is the opposite of what a catalyst does.

options.text: halogens
options.feedback: Halogens are reactive non-metals that take part in reactions and are used up in them.

parts.stem:
Zinc reacts with dilute sulfuric acid. The experiment is repeated with a more concentrated acid at the same temperature.

the acid particles are more closely packed, so collisions are more frequent and more successful collisions happen each second

any: more particles in the same volume

scheme.for: more particles in the same volume (the particles are closer together)
more frequent collisions / more successful collisions per unit time

hints: Concentration is about how many particles are in the space, not how fast they go.
There is no energy line in a concentration answer.
parts.workedSolution: There are more acid particles in the same volume, so the particles collide more frequently and there are more successful collisions per unit time.

commonErrors.feedback: Say more frequent collisions, or more successful collisions per unit time. 'More collisions' on its own is the phrasing the scheme refuses.

parts.stem:
A cube of calcium carbonate of side 2 cm is cut into 8 equal cubes.
Calculate the total surface area of the 8 small cubes.

scheme.for: surface area of one small cube = 6 × 1² = 6 (cm²)
48 (cm²)

hints: Six faces on each small cube.
There are 8 small cubes altogether.
parts.workedSolution: One small cube has side 1 cm, so its surface area is 6 × 1² = 6 cm². For all 8: 8 × 6 = 48 cm².

commonErrors.feedback: That is the surface area of one small cube. Multiply by 8, because the cut made that many of them.
That is the surface area before the cut. Each cut exposes two faces that were inside the solid, so the total area goes up while the volume stays the same.

parts.stem:
The volume of calcium carbonate is unchanged at 8 cm³.
Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of the 8 small cubes, in cm⁻¹.

scheme.for: surface area ÷ volume
6 (cm⁻¹)

hints: Surface area on top, volume underneath.
parts.workedSolution: ratio = surface area ÷ volume = 48 ÷ 8 = 6 cm⁻¹, against 3 cm⁻¹ for the whole cube.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the volume divided by the surface area. Written that way the number falls as the pieces get smaller, which is the wrong way round for this comparison.

parts.stem: Explain why the small cubes react faster with dilute hydrochloric acid than the single large cube.

accepted: the small cubes have a larger surface area to volume ratio, so acid particles collide with the solid more frequently and there are more successful collisions per unit time
a bigger surface area is exposed, so collisions are more frequent and more of them are successful each second

any: larger surface area to volume ratio

scheme.for: larger surface area (to volume ratio), so more of the solid is exposed to the acid
more frequent collisions / more successful collisions per unit time

hints: Use your ratio as the evidence, then finish in collision language.
parts.workedSolution: The small cubes have a larger surface area to volume ratio, so more of the calcium carbonate is exposed. Acid particles collide with the solid more frequently, and there are more successful collisions per unit time.

commonErrors.feedback: The amount of calcium carbonate is the same; only how much of it is exposed has changed. Compare the surface area to volume ratios, not the amounts.

of lower activation energy

parts.stem:
A catalyst is added to a reaction between marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid. Everything else is kept the same.
Explain why the total volume of carbon dioxide collected is unchanged.

accepted: the catalyst only changes how fast the reaction happens, and the amounts of reactant are the same, so the same volume of carbon dioxide is made
a catalyst changes the rate but not the amounts of reactant, so the same amount of gas is produced

scheme.for: a catalyst changes only the rate of the reaction
the amounts of reactant are unchanged, so the same amount of product forms

hints: Look at where the three curves finish, not how steep they are.
What decides how much gas can be made?
parts.workedSolution: A catalyst only changes the rate of the reaction. The amounts of reactant are unchanged, so the same amount of carbon dioxide is produced — it simply arrives sooner.

commonErrors.feedback: A faster reaction makes the same gas sooner, not more of it. On the graph the steeper curve levels off at exactly the same height.

parts.stem: In the four boxes shown, which change alters both how often the particles collide and the share of collisions that succeed?

options.text: raising the temperature
options.feedback: Both counts move: the particles meet more often and a bigger share of the meetings have enough energy.

options.text: making the solution more concentrated
options.feedback: Concentration changes only how often they meet. The share that succeed stays the same, which is why it is worth one mark and temperature two.

options.text: grinding the solid into a powder
options.feedback: Surface area works like concentration: more meetings, same share succeeding.

options.text: adding a catalyst
options.feedback: A catalyst leaves the number of collisions alone and raises the share that succeed, so it changes one of the two counts, not both.

scheme.for: raising the temperature

hints: Compare the two counters printed under each box.
parts.workedSolution: Raising the temperature: the collisions a second go from 20 to 40, and the successful ones from 2 to 8.

parts.stem: Which change leaves the number of collisions a second unaltered but raises the number that succeed?

options.text: adding a catalyst
options.feedback: The collisions stay at 20 a second, but 8 of them now succeed instead of 2, because the energy needed is lower.

options.text: raising the temperature
options.feedback: Heating raises both counts, so it is not the one that leaves the collisions alone.

options.text: making the solution more concentrated
options.feedback: Concentration raises the number of collisions; the share that succeed does not move.

options.text: using larger lumps of the solid
options.feedback: Larger lumps expose less surface, so there are fewer collisions and the reaction is slower.

scheme.for: adding a catalyst

hints: One box changes only the bottom counter.
parts.workedSolution: A catalyst: box D keeps 20 collisions a second, the same as box A, but 8 succeed instead of 2.

fewer successful collisions (per unit time)

parts.stem:
Marble chips react with dilute hydrochloric acid. The reaction can be made faster by warming the acid, by using a more concentrated acid, or by grinding the chips to a powder.
Explain, in terms of collisions between particles, how each of these three changes increases the rate of reaction.
This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist chemical terms used widely and accurately; organised with clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist chemical vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the intended meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: A reaction happens only when particles collide.
A collision succeeds only if the particles have at least the activation energy.
Warming the acid makes the particles move faster, so they collide more frequently.
Warming also means a greater proportion of collisions have energy at or above the activation energy.
keyWords: at or above the activation energy
more energy than the activation energy

indicativeContent.point: A more concentrated acid has more particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent.
keyWords: more particles in the same volume

indicativeContent.point: Powder has a larger surface area, so more of the solid is exposed and collisions are more frequent.
In every case the result is more successful collisions per unit time.

scheme.for: a banded explanation of all three changes in collision terms: collisions must happen, they must reach the activation energy, temperature raises both the frequency and the proportion with enough energy, concentration and surface area raise the frequency, and every route ends in more successful collisions per unit time
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Three changes, and the same two ideas each time: how often, and how hard.
Only one of the three changes the energy as well as the frequency.
parts.workedSolution: Particles can only react when they collide, and a collision only succeeds if the particles have at least the activation energy. Warming the acid makes the particles move faster, so they collide more frequently and a greater proportion of the collisions have energy at or above the activation energy. A more concentrated acid has more particles in the same volume, so the particles collide more frequently. Grinding the chips to a powder gives a larger surface area, so more of the marble is exposed and the acid particles collide with it more frequently. In every case there are more successful collisions per unit time, so the rate of reaction increases.

findTheMistake.stem:
Eabha is asked: 'State the effect of raising the temperature on the rate of reaction, and explain it in terms of particles. [3]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: The particles have more energy and move faster.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The effect is right and the particle line is right. The last line is the one the scheme refuses: 'more collisions' says nothing about whether those collisions reach the activation energy, and Summer 2025's report records it earning nothing.
correction: So there are more successful collisions per unit time.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the three marks: the effect and the particle energy both stand. The third needs one adjective and one phrase — more successful collisions per unit time. Write those five words the same way every time and this mark never goes again.

findTheMistake.stem:
Cathal is asked: 'Manganese(IV) oxide is added to hydrogen peroxide solution. State the effect this has on the reaction, and explain how it has that effect. [3]'
His answer:
studentWorking: A catalyst is a substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.
It provides an alternative reaction pathway.
This pathway has a lower activation energy.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The explanation is complete and correct. The opening line answers a question that was not asked: 'state the effect' wants what happens to this reaction — the rate of decomposition increases — not the definition of a catalyst. Summer 2025's report names this exact substitution.
correction: It increases the rate of decomposition of the hydrogen peroxide.
findTheMistake.feedback: The two explanation marks are safe. The one that goes is the effect, because a definition is not an effect. Read the command word first: state wants the change to the reaction, explain wants the pathway and the activation energy.

findTheMistake.stem:
Saoirse is asked: 'A catalyst is added to a reaction between marble chips and acid. Explain what happens to the rate and to the total volume of gas collected. [3]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: The rate of reaction increases, because the catalyst lowers the activation energy.
The total volume of gas collected is larger.
The reaction is faster than it was without the catalyst.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The rate half is right. The total volume is not: the amounts of marble and acid have not changed, so the same carbon dioxide is made either way. A catalyst changes when the gas arrives, not how much of it there is.
correction: The total volume of gas collected is unchanged: the amounts of reactant are the same, so the gas simply arrives sooner.
findTheMistake.feedback: One of the three: the rate and the activation energy are right. Picture the three curves from the rates lesson — different steepnesses, the same finishing height. Steeper means sooner, never more.

prompts.answer: The minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur.

prompts.prompt: What makes a collision between particles a successful one?
prompts.answer: The particles collide with energy at or above the activation energy, so they react instead of bouncing apart.

prompts.prompt: Write the phrase the mark scheme wants at the end of every rate explanation.
prompts.answer: More (or fewer) successful collisions per unit time.

prompts.prompt: Raising the temperature does two things to the collisions. What are they?
prompts.answer: The particles collide more frequently, and a greater proportion of the collisions have energy at or above the activation energy.

prompts.prompt: Raising the concentration does only one thing to the collisions. What is it, and why only one?
prompts.answer: Collisions become more frequent, because there are more particles in the same volume. Their energy is unchanged, because they are not moving any faster.
keyWords: more particles in the same volume

prompts.prompt: A cube of side 2 cm is cut into 8 equal cubes. What happens to the surface area, the volume and the rate?
prompts.answer: The surface area doubles from 24 to 48 cm², the volume stays at 8 cm³, so the surface area to volume ratio rises from 3 to 6 cm⁻¹ and the reaction is faster.

prompts.prompt: What is a catalyst, and what kind of substance is usually used as one?
prompts.answer: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being used up. Transition metals and their compounds are often used.

prompts.prompt: Name the catalyst used for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, and say what it looks like.
How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
prompts.answer: It provides an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful.

prompts.prompt: A catalyst is added. What happens to the energy change of the reaction, and to the total amount of product?
prompts.answer: Neither changes. The profile starts and finishes at the same levels, and the amounts of reactant decide the amount of product; only the activation energy and the time taken are different.

prompts.prompt: A table gives the mass of a solid before and after a reaction. How do you tell whether it was the catalyst?
prompts.answer: Its mass is the same before and after, and the reaction was faster than without it. A catalyst is also absent from the balanced equation.

prompts.prompt: On a reaction profile, which arrow is the activation energy and which is the energy change?
prompts.answer: Arrow (i) is the activation energy: the climb from the reactant level to the top of the hump. Arrow (ii) is the energy change: the gap between the reactant level and the product level.

findings.asked: Explain what a lower temperature does to the rate; name the catalyst used with hydrogen peroxide and explain how it works.
findings.wentWrong: Marks needed particles with less energy and fewer successful collisions; an answer resting on 'less collisions' earned nothing, and per unit time is expected from the next series. Manganese(IV) oxide defeated a significant number, and the definition of a catalyst was often given where its effect on the rate was wanted.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Stated the effect in one clause, then gave the particle energy and the successful collisions per unit time; and, for the catalyst, gave the effect first and the alternative pathway of lower activation energy second.
findings.rule: Fewer successful collisions per unit time; a catalyst speeds the reaction by providing an alternative pathway of lower activation energy.

findings.asked: The preparation of oxygen from hydrogen peroxide: apparatus, equation, catalyst and test.
findings.wentWrong: Naming the apparatus and writing the equation were the hard parts; most named the catalyst here, but many said oxygen relights a lit splint rather than a glowing one.
findings.rule: Manganese(IV) oxide catalyses the decomposition; oxygen relights a glowing splint.

findings.asked: The same oxygen preparation at Foundation, with state symbols.
findings.wentWrong: Apparatus names and state symbols were very challenging; few identified the catalyst; the lit-splint error appeared again.
findings.rule: Learn the named catalyst and the three gas tests as fixed phrases.

findings.asked: A six-mark extended answer that included the definition of activation energy and the energy change of the thermite reaction.
findings.wentWrong: The definition of activation energy was usually right and the energy change was named, but the reason behind that change was rarely given.
findings.rule: Activation energy is the minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur; the energy change is the gap between the reactant and product levels, and a catalyst alters neither end.

insight.ruleToRemember: Rate is about collisions. Temperature changes two things (more frequent collisions, and a greater proportion with energy at or above the activation energy); concentration and surface area change one (more frequent collisions). A catalyst increases the rate without being used up by providing an alternative pathway of lower activation energy, and manganese(IV) oxide is the one CCEA names. Every explanation ends in more or fewer successful collisions per unit time, and none of these changes alters how much product is made.
insight.aStarSignal: Explaining a change with frequency AND energy where both apply, writing 'successful collisions per unit time' every time, and describing a catalyst's effect on the rate rather than reciting its definition.
